identity.title: One for Two: A Unified Framework for Imbalanced Graph Classification via Dynamic Balanced Prototype

problem.claim: Graph classification remains vulnerable to graph-level class and topological imbalance.

contributions.claim: UniImb unifies treatment of class and topological imbalance through personalized graph perturbations, dynamic balanced prototypes, and prototype load balancing.
The abstract reports an Information Bottleneck-based theoretical justification for these design choices.
The authors report releasing AirGraph, a large-scale imbalanced air-pollution graph dataset.

stated_novelty.claim: The stated distinction is a unified framework addressing both class and topological graph-level imbalance.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report dominant performance across various imbalanced scenarios on 19 datasets against 23 baselines, including AirGraph.
The authors report that AirGraph was released with the work.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNN-based graph classification is described as vulnerable to class and topological imbalance.
UniImb is introduced as a unified response to both imbalance types.
The framework combines multi-scale topology, learnable personalized perturbations, dynamic balanced prototypes, and load-balancing optimization.
The design is theoretically motivated by Information Bottleneck, then reported experiments span 19 datasets and 23 baselines.
The authors state that code is available on GitHub.

source_observation.claim: The abstract names two imbalance sources and maps them to distinct mechanisms within one framework: topology-aware perturbation, balanced prototypes, and majority-dominance mitigation.

lessons.interpretation: Explicitly aligning each problem dimension with a mechanism can make a unified-method claim easier to evaluate conceptually.
lessons.application: For a multi-factor learning problem, state the factors separately and identify which module or objective addresses each one.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the factors are not independently characterized or when one mechanism genuinely handles all factors without meaningful specialization.

unknowns: The abstract provides no quantitative performance values, dataset-wise results, or statistical details behind “dominant performance.”
The theoretical justification’s assumptions and conclusions are unspecified; the abstract does not establish proof correctness.
